sections.title: Data Engineering Services ClickMasters Provides
sections.description: End-to-end data infrastructure for production ML.

blocks.heading: ETL and Data Pipeline Development
paragraphs: Moving data from where it lives to where ML needs it:

Source system integration: Connecting to operational data sources (Salesforce, Workday, Epic FHIR, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Kafka, Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift) with the reliability and monitoring that production ML pipelines require. Most ML projects require integrating 3–10 data sources — each integration has its own authentication, rate limiting, schema evolution challenges, and failure modes.

Data quality and validation: Building data quality checks into pipelines — detecting null values, out-of-range values, unexpected schema changes, and data drift before bad data reaches models. Production ML without data quality monitoring produces silent failures — models continue generating predictions from wrong inputs without raising visible errors until someone notices that business metrics have degraded.

Historical backfill: For new ML pipelines, loading historical data for model training — typically 12–36 months of historical data — requires backfill pipeline design that doesn't overwhelm source systems or violate rate limits while building the training dataset.
Cost: $20,000–$70,000 | Timeline: 6–14 weeks

blocks.heading: Feature Engineering Pipelines
paragraphs: Transforming raw data into the ML features that actually predict:

Feature computation: The transformation of raw data into predictive signals — recency-frequency-monetary (RFM) calculations for customer analytics, rolling window aggregations for time-series features, text embedding computation for NLP features, and graph features for network-based ML. Feature engineering typically accounts for 70–80% of ML project effort and most of the performance difference between models.

Feature stores: Infrastructure that computes features once and serves them consistently to both model training and real-time inference — preventing the feature inconsistency (training-serving skew) that occurs when features are computed differently during offline training and online serving.

Point-in-time correct features: For fraud detection, churn prediction, and risk models where historical prediction accuracy testing matters, pipeline design must ensure that features are computed from data that was actually available at prediction time — preventing future data leakage that causes models to appear more accurate on historical data than they'll be in production.
Cost: $25,000–$75,000 | Timeline: 8–16 weeks

blocks.heading: MLOps and Model Deployment Infrastructure
paragraphs: Automating the model development, validation, and deployment lifecycle:

ML training pipelines: Automated, reproducible model training pipelines that — given a dataset and hyperparameter configuration — train a model, evaluate its performance, and log results to an experiment tracker (MLflow, Weights & Biases). Automated training pipelines eliminate the 'it works on my laptop' problem and enable parallel hyperparameter search.

Model registry and versioning: Centralized storage of trained models with version control, performance metadata, and deployment history — enabling teams to roll back to previous model versions when new versions underperform in production, and ensuring that the model artifact deployed in production is exactly the one that was validated.

Continuous integration and deployment for ML: Automated model testing and deployment triggered by code commits or scheduled retraining — the ML equivalent of CI/CD for software that enables teams to iterate on models rapidly while maintaining production reliability.

Model serving infrastructure: REST API or gRPC model serving with the latency, throughput, and availability that production applications require — from simple Flask/FastAPI wrapping for low-volume batch prediction to NVIDIA Triton or TorchServe for high-throughput real-time serving.
Cost: $30,000–$90,000 | Timeline: 8–18 weeks

blocks.heading: Real-Time Streaming Pipelines
paragraphs: ML from event streams rather than batch data:

Kafka and event stream integration: Consuming from Kafka, Kinesis, or Pub/Sub event streams for real-time ML feature computation — aggregating events in real time to compute features like 'transactions in the last 5 minutes' for fraud detection or 'page views in the last hour' for recommendation.

Real-time feature computation: Low-latency feature computation from event streams for fraud detection, recommendation, and personalization applications where prediction latency must be under 100ms from event receipt to prediction delivery.

Stream processing frameworks: Apache Flink, Spark Streaming, and Kafka Streams for real-time pipeline development — selecting the right framework for throughput, latency, and operational complexity trade-offs.
Cost: $35,000–$100,000 | Timeline: 10–20 weeks

blocks.heading: Data Lake and Warehouse Architecture
paragraphs: The data foundation that ML pipelines run on:

Data lake design: S3, GCS, or Azure Data Lake storage architecture for ML — organizing raw, processed, and feature-ready data in a layered architecture (bronze/silver/gold or raw/cleaned/features) that enables ML pipeline development without constant data archaeology.

dbt for feature transformation: dbt (data build tool) pipelines for SQL-based feature engineering — enabling data transformation with the software engineering practices (version control, testing, documentation) that reliable ML pipelines require.
Lakehouse architecture: Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, or Apache Hudi for ACID transaction support in data lakes — enabling ML pipeline updates and corrections without rebuilding entire datasets.
Cost: $25,000–$80,000 | Timeline: 8–16 weeks

sections.title: ClickMasters' Data Engineering Stack
sections.description: The modern data engineering tools we use to build production ML infrastructure.

blocks.heading: Orchestration
paragraphs: Apache Airflow, Prefect, and Dagster for pipeline scheduling, dependency management, and failure alerting — ClickMasters defaults to Airflow for enterprise clients with existing Airflow deployments and Prefect for new builds where modern ergonomics matter.

blocks.heading: Feature Stores
paragraphs: Feast (open-source), Tecton, and Hopsworks for production feature store deployment — ClickMasters recommends based on existing cloud infrastructure and team familiarity.

blocks.heading: Streaming
paragraphs: Apache Kafka, AWS Kinesis, and Apache Flink for real-time pipeline development.

blocks.heading: Storage
paragraphs: Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, and Delta Lake for analytical storage; Redis and DynamoDB for low-latency feature serving.

blocks.heading: MLOps
paragraphs: MLflow for experiment tracking and model registry; Kubeflow or SageMaker Pipelines for ML workflow orchestration; FastAPI and NVIDIA Triton for model serving.

items.question: What's the minimum data engineering budget?
items.answer: $20,000 for a targeted ETL pipeline from defined sources to a target ML training dataset. Production-grade MLOps infrastructure: $30,000–$60,000.

items.question: Can ClickMasters build on existing cloud infrastructure (AWS, Azure, GCP)?
items.answer: Yes — ClickMasters designs data engineering on your existing cloud infrastructure. We don't require greenfield environments and don't have cloud platform partnerships that bias our recommendations.

items.question: How long does ML data infrastructure take?
items.answer: 6–20 weeks depending on scope. Basic ETL: 6–10 weeks. Full MLOps with feature store and real-time serving: 16–20 weeks.

items.question: What causes training-serving skew and how does ClickMasters prevent it?
items.answer: Training-serving skew occurs when features are computed differently during model training and online prediction. ClickMasters prevents it by using the same feature computation code in both training and serving pipelines — typically through a feature store that serves both contexts from the same feature definitions.

items.question: Does ClickMasters provide ongoing data pipeline maintenance?
items.answer: ClickMasters delivers pipelines that your team can maintain — with documentation, runbooks, and operational monitoring dashboards. Ongoing managed support is available at a monthly retainer; most clients maintain pipelines internally after a 4–8 week knowledge transfer.

items.question: Do we own the data pipeline code after delivery?
items.answer: Yes — complete IP transfer at project close including pipeline code, infrastructure-as-code, documentation, and test suites.
